user_prompt: How can I help students understand the application of the theorem for determining line-plane perpendicularity (reverse construction)?
context: In a senior secondary geometry lesson, students are applying the theorem: a line is parallel to a plane if it is parallel to a line in that plane. The teacher projects a prism problem: prove that a segment joining two edge midpoints is parallel to one of the base planes. The diagram shows no existing line in the target plane that is visibly parallel to the given segment. Students copy the diagram but wait for the teacher to add the missing line. The teacher wants to shift from demonstrating the proof to making the construction process visible. The trigger moment occurs when a student asks, 'How did you know to draw that line?' The teacher responds by reverse reasoning: to prove line-plane parallel, we need line-line parallel; the figure does not give it, so we must construct it. The class discusses what geometric clues are present, such as midpoints and parallelogram properties, and how these clues suggest a midsegment or a constructed parallelogram. The teacher withholds the actual auxiliary line and instead asks the class to propose which points to connect and why. The goal is to help students see auxiliary lines not as magic but as the result of a search strategy.
expected_output: A satisfactory response must show the complete reverse construction process. First, the teacher restates the goal: to prove line l is parallel to plane α, find a line m in α with l parallel to m. The teacher then examines the figure and points out that no such line is given. The teacher asks students to identify usable features, such as midpoints or pairs of equal and parallel segments, and proposes two strategies: if two midpoints of a triangle are available, connect them to form a midsegment; if no parallel line exists, construct a parallelogram by connecting selected points. The teacher demonstrates the chosen construction step by step, writing 'connect ... to ...' before proving, and then proves the constructed line is parallel to the given line and lies in the plane. The response should end with a summary of the two models: the midpoint-midsegment model and the parallelogram model, plus the logical requirement that construction comes before proof. This equips students to transfer the strategy to new figures.

She wants to avoid vague responses such as 'be more careful' or 'review the concept.' For derivative extrema, have them make a sign chart and compare endpoints, labeling local versus global. For sequence summation, ask them to write the first three and last two terms before cancelling and check index alignment. For analytic geometry, ask them to re-substitute the simplified equation into the original system and state what the discriminant sign means. For probability, have students label objects and decide whether order changes the event before choosing permutations or combinations. For inequality always-true problems, ask them to test boundary values and check sign before dividing by a parameter. For SSA triangles, have them sketch both possible arcs and compare the side with the height. For complex numbers, ask them to rewrite z times z-bar as the square of the modulus and compute modulus first. For solid geometry, have them re-derive coordinates from a labeled vertex and re-check vector coordinates before dot products. Each diagnosis should end with one concrete micro-fix and record the symptom, root cause, and fix in an error-pattern library. The answer should avoid vague feedback and aim to expose contradictions through student re-substitution.

user_prompt: How can I clearly explain the distribution problem of putting identical elements into different boxes (the stars-and-bars method)?

Several children, including a student called Xiaoyu, sigh when homework is assigned, avoid starting, and often say, “I’m just not good at this.” They leave tasks incomplete, become teary or frustrated, and seem to believe effort will not help. The behavior has lasted for weeks and now appears across subjects. Some families report daily homework battles; other teachers have also voiced concern. Ms. Lin wants to intervene early, but she is unsure how to identify the underlying pattern of chronic homework resistance and learned helplessness. She needs a practical classroom plan that helps her observe warning signs, investigate causes without labeling children, design small achievable assignments, use positive feedback, support children’s emotions, guide parents, and coordinate with subject teachers. I want to design a local "Soil in Our Hometown" project that is simple enough for Grade 3 students. I also need to manage classroom time because some groups work fast while others work slowly; if I enforce the same pace, slower groups cannot finish while faster groups lose interest. In the past, students threw away their products and lost their recording sheets, so no evidence remained. I want them to record and keep materials, and I want every child, including quiet or struggling students, to have a role and participate. The answer must break the project into 4-6 single-lesson microtasks, each with clear operations: observe and collect local soil samples, record properties, compare samples, design a simple test, and present findings. It must include basic skill scaffolds such as drawing, measuring, and connecting materials for students with weak hands-on skills. For 45 students in 11 groups, it must assign fixed roles such as leader, recorder, material manager, and reporter so every student participates. It must provide ready-to-print recording sheets and assign a record keeper to prevent lost materials. It must describe a three-level check: self-assessment, peer review, and group acceptance. Finally, it should include simple process evaluation and support quiet or struggling students.

user_prompt: In first grade, during the "colorful paper chain" craft, a student doesn't know how to cut a straight line with scissors; the cut goes crooked as soon as he cuts. He hands me the scissors directly and says, "Teacher, you cut it for me." How should I guide him to complete it himself?
context: In an elementary science classroom, students regularly work on hands-on tasks that require fine motor control, observation, and troubleshooting. Many children, when a material does not behave as expected, immediately seek adult intervention: they hand over scissors, say 'I can't,' or abandon a project. The teacher wants to use scaffolded instruction aligned with Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and elementary science standards. The goal is to help students identify the precise difficulty, try a smaller or adjusted step, compare outcomes, and return to independent work—without the teacher doing the task, giving a ready-made answer, or dismissing student ideas. The following scenarios occur across early elementary grades: cutting straight lines for a paper chain; troubleshooting a circuit; improving a paper bridge; measuring a desk with a flexible tape; adjusting a water filter; using a magnifier; aligning wheels on a wind car; labeling rock specimens; simplifying a paper house design; and managing overflow in a baking soda-vinegar reaction. In each case, the teacher must choose words and demonstrations that provide the least support necessary while maintaining safety and preserving student agency.
expected_output: A satisfactory response should name the specific skill or conceptual gap, then provide a low-intervention scaffold that lets the student act. For example, the teacher might ask the child to compare two attempts, point to one changeable part, model only a small segment, or use a guiding question such as 'What did you notice when...?' The teacher should not cut, wire, build, or measure for the student. When safety is involved, the teacher may demonstrate a safe technique or steady the object, but the student should handle the main action. The response should include a brief check for understanding and an invitation to try again, followed by reflection: 'What changed?' or 'What will you try next?' Scaffolds should match the grade level: for younger students, use concrete cues, simple choices, and a visible model; for older students, use targeted questions and evidence from the attempt. The answer may include possible causes and one or two scaffolded prompts, but must avoid giving the full solution. It should also preserve student confidence by framing mistakes as information and leaving the student's own design or idea valued.

It should address grade-specific needs: for grades 1-2, use chants, demonstrations, and turn-taking games; for grades 3-6, support student-made rules and orderly transition from teacher-directed to autonomous group work. Finally, it should comply with education regulations and protect student dignity and safety.

It focuses on controlling total workload across subjects, converting paper drills into practical tasks, running real projects with fair individual accountability, and designing layered fallback pathways. The trigger scenarios are drawn from ten common school situations. A teaching group leader finds 30 minutes of drafting, 40 minutes of calculations, and 40 minutes of CNC coding assigned on the same afternoon, causing overload. A specialized teacher shifts to a four-person CNC lathe operation video but needs hard role rotation. A homeroom teacher must create a legal non-social alternative for a severe-social-anxiety student. A teacher hears a group leader report two non-contributing members one week before submission. A supervisor needs a two-dimension grading table with objective evidence. A department head faces teacher fear of marking real project calculations. An electrical teacher must use one set of soldering equipment for three ability levels. A peer review is distorted by friendship scoring. A course developer wants last year's campus energy data turned into a reusable question bank. A vice principal must answer a parent who believes practical projects are worse than paper tests.
expected_output: A satisfactory answer must give concrete tools, not general advice. For overload, it should supply a daily cross-subject homework load log with hard caps and a shared cut rule: keep only one exercise per repeated knowledge point, reject over-limit work. For video tasks, set fixed rotating roles such as operator, procedure checker, safety observer, and recorder, with visible rotation evidence. For social anxiety, create a legal single-person substitute such as an individual flow diagram, simulation log, or recorded report that tests the same core skill. For group freeloading, intervene with clear task redistribution, short deadlines, and individual contribution evidence before grading. For group fairness, use a two-dimension rubric covering individual process and group product, with objective evidence fields: uploaded revision timestamps, task photos or screenshots, and question-response records. For project anxiety, bring in an enterprise practitioner to calibrate and use method-and-evidence marking with acceptable ranges. For mixed ability, set basic, improvement, and innovation tasks on the same soldering equipment. For peer review, require two observed objective facts and one improvement point before a score. For reusing project data, convert last year's energy data into standardized cases, blanks, and benchmarks. For parents, explain that practical projects test search, tool use, judgment, and vocational skill application, which align with the skill certificate and workplace better than fill-in-the-blank questions.
